title: Choose a gorilla trek by the park system and your limits
description: Compare Rwanda and Uganda gorilla trekking through official permit and briefing routes, physical demands and wildlife rules before you commit.
intent: How do I compare a Rwanda or Uganda gorilla trek responsibly, without assuming the same permits, rules or trail conditions apply in both countries?

sections.heading: Choose a country before choosing a lodge
paragraphs: Gorilla trekking in Rwanda and Uganda is not one interchangeable product. The official Rwanda Development Board booking page describes Volcanoes National Park, its Kinigi briefing point and permit process. Uganda’s permits and park management are handled separately by the Uganda Wildlife Authority. UWA’s July 2024 guidelines name Bwindi Impenetrable and Mgahinga Gorilla National Parks and five tracking entry sectors; they say permits are booked by date and entry point, while the gorilla family is allocated on the day as the animals move. Verify current arrangements with UWA before booking. Compare each country’s current official booking instructions, park, transfer route, cancellation policy and operator before using a travel blog or lodge page to decide.

A useful comparison sheet has separate columns for Rwanda and Uganda: official permit authority, park and meeting location, exact date availability, what transport is included, how changes are handled, and what medical or mobility questions you need answered. Do not assume a permit from one country gives access in the other or that a named gorilla family will be assigned in advance.

sections.heading: Treat the briefing as part of the experience
paragraphs: Rwanda’s tourism authority states that trekkers report to the Kinigi offices for a briefing and gives current practical notes on clothing, rain gear, water and camera flash. It also says tracking is for people aged 15 or older under its published rules. Read the current official terms for the country you choose rather than applying Rwanda’s age rule to Uganda or assuming a copied itinerary remains valid.

Ask the authority or licensed operator how the day is structured: where you check in, when to arrive, which items to carry and what can change if the gorilla group moves. The walk can take longer or be more demanding than expected, and RDB notes that high altitude may cause difficulty for some visitors. If that raises a health or mobility concern, discuss the specific trek with a clinician and the official operator before paying.

sections.heading: Protect the gorillas and your own wellbeing
paragraphs: Follow the assigned guide’s directions, keep your movement calm, do not touch or feed gorillas, and never use flash where prohibited. RDB’s published instructions tell visitors not to make rapid movements and to follow the guide if an animal charges or vocalizes. These are wildlife safeguards, not theatrical rules. Keep a respectful distance as instructed on the day and let the gorillas decide how they move through the forest.

Because great apes can be vulnerable to human illness, do not trek if you are unwell; ask the park authority about its current health screening and visitor protocols. Carry only what the authority permits and avoid eating or drinking near the gorillas where its rules prohibit it. For your own safety, do not treat a porter, guide or group pace as medical advice; communicate limitations early and follow professional guidance.

sections.heading: Compare access and support, not just price
paragraphs: RDB’s Rwanda page identifies a route from Kigali to Musanze and then Kinigi, and notes that the trek begins with a scheduled briefing. Ask what the quoted package includes between airport, lodging, park and check-in. For Uganda, verify the specific park and transport with UWA or its authorized booking channels. A cheaper headline may leave you responsible for a separate permit, transfer or overnight near the trailhead.

Read cancellation and refund terms directly from the issuing authority. Rwanda’s page describes different treatment for a day when a group cannot be found versus a late arrival or unrelated cancellation. Do not assume another country or operator has the same terms. Leave a buffer night near the park instead of making the trek dependent on a same-day international arrival.

sections.heading: Make a decision that fits the actual trek
paragraphs: Choose the trek only after you can answer four questions: which country and park, which official permit is confirmed, how you will reach the briefing, and what support exists if you cannot continue. If a booking page or operator cannot answer those plainly, pause and contact the relevant wildlife authority. Consider a shorter guided forest walk or another wildlife experience if the physical or logistical demands do not fit your circumstances.

The RDB page is primary for Rwanda but does not establish Uganda’s rules or current conditions there. This article makes no promise about permit availability, group assignment, sighting or trail duration. Check each country’s official guidance close to travel, and make your choice around an informed, respectful visit rather than a guaranteed close encounter.

sources.title: Mountain gorilla tracking
sources.purpose: Supports Rwanda’s Volcanoes National Park booking, Kinigi briefing, age rule, travel logistics, published visitor conduct and note that altitude/trek effort can challenge some visitors.

sources.title: Guidelines for the Management of Gorilla / Chimpanzee Tracking and Other Tourism Products
sources.purpose: Supports the Uganda-specific distinction: the July 2024 guidelines name Bwindi and Mgahinga, designate five tracking entry sectors, state permits are booked by date/entry point, and gorilla families are allocated on the day. Recheck current official arrangements before travel.
